name: OS Credential Dumping
overview: Adversaries attempt to extract credentials from operating system caches, memory, or on-disk data structures such as the SAM database, LSASS process memory, or the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit). Credentials are typically recovered in hash or plaintext form and used for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or persistence via pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, or offline cracking. Each sub-technique below targets a distinct extraction surface: process memory, an on-disk credential database, a registry secret store, or the flat credential files that mirror these same primitives on Linux.

prerequisite_concepts.explanation: A protected Windows process (lsass.exe) that authenticates logons and holds the resulting credential material — NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and in older/misconfigured setups even reversible or plaintext secrets — in memory for the duration of a session. It is the single highest-value memory target on any Windows host, which is why T1003.001 exists as its own sub-technique.

NTLM hash (a fixed hash of the password, reusable directly via pass-the-hash without ever knowing the plaintext); Kerberos ticket / TGT (a time-bound token that can be replayed via pass-the-ticket, or a krbtgt hash that can forge new tickets — a Golden Ticket); DCC2 / MSCache v2 (a salted, iterated hash of a domain logon cached for offline use — cannot be pass-the-hash'd, only cracked offline); plaintext (recoverable only if WDigest or a similar legacy provider is enabled, or from an application that mishandles secrets in memory).

The SAM (Security Account Manager) database holds *local* accounts for a single machine, at %SystemRoot%\System32\config\SAM. NTDS.dit is its domain-wide equivalent — the full Active Directory database, living only on domain controllers — and dumping it exposes every domain account at once, not just one host's local accounts.

A hive is an on-disk file backing a section of the Windows Registry. SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY are each separate hive files; SYSTEM holds the boot key needed to decrypt secrets in the other two, which is why adversaries almost always export all three together with reg save rather than just one.

Most of these sub-techniques need SYSTEM or local-Administrator rights on the target host (T1003.001–.005, .007, .008). DCSync (T1003.006) is different: it needs no code execution on a domain controller at all, only an account holding the Replicating Directory Changes / Replicating Directory Changes All AD permissions — normally Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and DC computer accounts.

Windows does not log handle or read access to files and registry keys (Security 4656/4663) by default — it requires an explicit System Access Control List on the object plus the "Audit Object Access" policy enabled. Most of the file/registry-based detections in this guide only produce telemetry if this auditing was deliberately turned on beforehand; verify it's enabled before relying on those event IDs in your own environment.

A Windows service that creates a point-in-time snapshot of a volume. Files that are normally locked while in use by the OS — like an active ntds.dit — can be read freely from a shadow copy, which is why vssadmin create shadow shows up repeatedly in NTDS and SAM extraction procedures as a way around file locks.

The RPC interface domain controllers use to replicate directory data with each other. DCSync works by calling this same interface from a non-DC host and asking a real DC to "replicate" account data to it — the DC has no way to tell the request isn't coming from a legitimate peer DC, which is why the defense is access-control on who holds replication rights, not the protocol itself.

A pseudo-filesystem that exposes live kernel and process state as if it were files. /proc/<PID>/maps shows a process's memory layout; /proc/<PID>/mem is a direct read/write window into that same memory. Root can read any process this way, making it the closest Linux equivalent of dumping LSASS.

/etc/passwd is world-readable and holds account metadata only (no hashes since the shadow-password scheme replaced inline hashes decades ago). /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is root-only (mode 0600) by default — the two files must be combined (e.g. with unshadow) before offline cracking tools can use them.

subtechniques.name: LSASS Memory
subtechniques.overview: The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) holds credential material generated during user logon in process memory. With administrative or SYSTEM-level access, an adversary can open a handle to lsass.exe and either harvest credentials in-memory or dump the process to disk for offline analysis with tools like Mimikatz. Common execution paths include Mimikatz's sekurlsa module, SysInternals-style procdump, the built-in comsvcs.dll MiniDump export invoked through rundll32.exe, and abuse of Windows Error Reporting (Silent Process Exit) to trigger a crash dump of LSASS on demand.

concepts.term: Why LSASS holds credentials at all: the SSP architecture
concepts.explanation: At startup LSASS loads a set of Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs — msv1_0.dll (NTLM), kerberos.dll (Kerberos), wdigest.dll (WDigest), tspkg.dll/livessp.dll (Terminal Services/live SSO) — and each one keeps its own copy of credential material in memory so the user isn't re-prompted for a password on every authentication (single sign-on). sekurlsa::logonPasswords in Mimikatz simply walks each SSP's internal memory structures and prints what it finds; it isn't exploiting a bug, it's reading data LSASS is deliberately keeping around for SSO.

concepts.term: Why some dumps show a plaintext password
concepts.explanation: WDigest, one of those SSPs, historically kept a reversibly-encrypted copy of the plaintext password (needed to answer HTTP Digest auth challenges). Since Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2, and via KB2871997 on backported older systems, the registry value HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential defaults to 0, which stops WDigest from caching it. A LSASS dump that yields plaintext almost always means this value was explicitly set back to 1, or the host predates the patch.

concepts.term: The GrantedAccess mask is the actual fingerprint
concepts.explanation: To read another process's memory, a caller needs a handle to it obtained via OpenProcess() with specific access rights (PROCESS_VM_READ, PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION, etc.), and Windows encodes exactly which rights were granted as a bitmask. Sysmon 10 logs that mask verbatim as GrantedAccess — values like 0x1010 or 0x1fffff aren't arbitrary detection strings, they're the literal access rights a credential-reading tool needs, which is why they're such a reliable signal.

concepts.term: Why file-based and API-based dumping produce the same result
concepts.explanation: Mimikatz's in-memory reading and the comsvcs.dll/procdump file-dumping route both ultimately rely on the same OS capability: a full memory snapshot of lsass.exe (via MiniDumpWriteDump in DbgHelp.dll, or equivalent direct memory reads). Once a .dmp file exists, it can be moved off-box and parsed offline with Mimikatz's minidump module with no live access to the original host required — this is why detecting the dump file's creation matters as much as detecting the initial process-access.

concepts.term: How Protected Process Light (PPL) actually stops this
concepts.explanation: Credential Guard and PPL work by marking lsass.exe itself as a protected process in the kernel. Once protected, even an Administrator-token process's OpenProcess() call against it is rejected outright by the kernel unless the calling process is itself signed and running as a protected process of equal or higher level — this is a kernel-enforced access check, not something a normal admin tool (including most dumping utilities) can bypass, which is why M1025/M1043 are the mitigations that actually change the threat model rather than just adding detection.

procedure_examples.activity: Used the plainpwd Mimikatz variant and rundll32.exe + comsvcs.dll to dump LSASS.
Deployed procdump against Exchange servers to harvest credentials post-compromise.
Targeted hashed credentials from LSASS memory as part of a living-off-the-land intrusion set.
Injects into or reads LSASS memory to extract password hashes via its built-in Mimikatz integration.
sekurlsa::Minidump and sekurlsa::logonPasswords modules parse LSASS memory for plaintext credentials and hashes.

data_sources.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe with a GrantedAccess mask indicative of full or memory-read rights (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff, 0x143a).
Handle requested / object access attempt on lsass.exe — requires object-level SACL auditing enabled on the process, not on by default.
Process creation for rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll and MiniDump on the command line, procdump.exe, or Task Manager's dump-file helper.
.dmp / .mdmp file creation in non-standard paths shortly after a LSASS handle event.

detection_queries.title: LSASS Memory Access (Defender for Endpoint)
detection_queries.description: Flags processes opening LSASS with access rights consistent with credential dumping, excluding common legitimate callers.
detection_queries.query:
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (
    "MsMpEng.exe", "csrss.exe", "wininit.exe", "services.exe",
    "svchost.exe", "lsm.exe", "taskmgr.exe", "procexp.exe", "procexp64.exe"
))
| extend GrantedAccess = tostring(AdditionalFields.GrantedAccess)
| where GrantedAccess in ("0x1010", "0x1410", "0x147a", "0x143a", "0x1fffff", "0x1f3fff")
    or GrantedAccess has_any ("0x10", "0x40")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GrantedAccess, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

subtechniques.name: Security Account Manager
subtechniques.overview: The SAM database holds local account credentials, normally enumerable only via APIs like net user. With SYSTEM-level access an adversary can extract it in-memory or export the underlying registry hives (HKLM\SAM, HKLM\SYSTEM) with reg save for offline parsing by tools such as Creddump7. Local RID 500 is the built-in Administrator, RID 501 is Guest, and RID 1000+ are regular local accounts — the values attackers are actually after.

concepts.term: Why SYSTEM is required, and why reg save still works
concepts.explanation: The SAM hive's registry key ACL restricts read access to the SYSTEM account only, and the file backing it is exclusively locked while Windows is running. reg save doesn't need to break that lock — it asks the registry subsystem itself (a kernel-mode API) for a consistent copy, which is why it works even while the OS is fully up, but it still fails without SYSTEM-equivalent rights because the ACL check happens regardless of the access method.

concepts.term: SYSKEY and why SYSTEM must be exported too
concepts.explanation: Hashes inside the SAM hive are not stored in the clear — they're encrypted with a per-machine boot key (introduced by the SYSKEY feature in NT4 SP3) that is itself scattered across obfuscated values in the SYSTEM hive. SAM alone is unusable ciphertext; every real-world extraction (Mimikatz, secretsdump.py, reg save scripts) grabs SAM and SYSTEM together specifically because SYSTEM supplies the key that unlocks SAM offline.

concepts.term: Why NTLM hashes are worth stealing directly
concepts.explanation: Unlike the salted DCC2 hashes covered under T1003.005, local NTLM hashes are unsalted — the same password always produces the same hash. That means a stolen NTLM hash doesn't need to be cracked at all; it can be replayed directly against any service that accepts NTLM authentication (pass-the-hash), which is why local SAM extraction is often a lateral-movement enabler even without ever recovering a plaintext password.

procedure_examples.activity: Executed reg save against SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives during the Nearest Neighbor campaign.
Acquired credentials from the SAM and SECURITY registry hives.
Dumps usernames and hashed passwords directly from SAM.
Extracts SAM hashes both locally and remotely via registry hive retrieval.
Credential Dumper module reads encrypted password hashes from HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F and the Users subkeys.

data_sources.detail: Handle/access events on HKLM\SAM — requires SACL auditing configured on the hive, not default.
reg.exe with save and a target of hklm\sam, hklm\system, or hklm\security on the command line.
.save / .hiv / .dmp files created by reg.exe or a copy command shortly after the reg save.

subtechniques.name: NTDS
subtechniques.overview: NTDS.dit, normally at %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit on a domain controller, is the Active Directory database and holds credential material for every domain account. Adversaries extract it via ntdsutil.exe's Install From Media (IFM) function, by creating a Volume Shadow Copy of the DC's volume and lifting the file directly, or remotely via Impacket's secretsdump.py over the DRSUAPI replication interface (which overlaps functionally with DCSync).

concepts.term: It's an ESE/JET database, not a proprietary format
concepts.explanation: ntds.dit is built on the Extensible Storage Engine (ESE, also called JET Blue) — the same database engine Exchange uses for mailbox stores. That's why generic ESE tooling like esentutl.exe can interact with it directly, and why offline parsers (Impacket's ntds parsing, DSInternals) can walk the same well-documented table structure rather than reverse-engineering something bespoke.

concepts.term: Why Volume Shadow Copy is the standard workaround
concepts.explanation: Like the SAM hive, ntds.dit is held open exclusively by the ntds.exe/lsass.exe service the entire time the DC is running, so it can't simply be copied. VSS solves this the way it solves it for any backup software: it creates a block-level, point-in-time snapshot of the whole volume, and files are read from that snapshot rather than the live, locked file — the copy operation never touches the actual in-use handle.

concepts.term: Two layers of encryption, same pattern as SAM
concepts.explanation: Values inside ntds.dit are encrypted with a Password Encryption Key (PEK) that is itself stored in the database but wrapped by the boot key from the DC's own SYSTEM registry hive. This mirrors the SAM/SYSTEM relationship exactly, which is why every real NTDS extraction — ntdsutil IFM, secretsdump, manual VSS copy — always grabs the SYSTEM hive alongside ntds.dit; without it the database is just encrypted bytes.

concepts.term: IFM is a legitimate feature being repurposed
concepts.explanation: ntdsutil's "ifm" (Install From Media) mode is a real, Microsoft-documented way to stand up a new domain controller without full network replication — it packages a consistent snapshot of ntds.dit plus the SYSTEM hive specifically so a new DC can be seeded offline. The abuse in this sub-technique isn't a flaw in IFM; it's using a legitimate provisioning feature for its side effect (a portable, ready-to-decrypt copy of every credential in the domain) rather than its intended purpose.

procedure_examples.activity: Used the built-in ntdsutil.exe to extract the AD database.
Extracted NTDS.dit by creating volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks.
Used ntdsutil.exe and vssadmin-created shadow copies during the Nearest Neighbor campaign.

subtechniques.name: LSA Secrets
subtechniques.overview: LSA Secrets, stored under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets, hold credential material Windows itself needs at boot before a user logs on — commonly service account passwords, scheduled task run-as credentials, and cached RDP/auto-logon passwords. SYSTEM-level access lets an adversary export the key with reg.exe or pull it from memory with Mimikatz's lsadump::secrets.

concepts.term: Why Windows needs a credential store nobody has logged into yet
concepts.explanation: Some things Windows must do before any human authenticates: start services configured to log on as a specific account, run scheduled tasks under a stored run-as identity, resolve an auto-logon password, or apply the machine account's own password for domain communication. None of those can wait for a user-specific decryption key, so Windows keeps this narrow set of secrets in a location LSA can decrypt to itself at boot — that location is exactly HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets.

concepts.term: Same boot-key protection as SAM and NTDS
concepts.explanation: LSA Secrets values are encrypted with a key derived from the same SYSTEM-hive boot key that protects SAM and NTDS.dit. A raw reg save of the SECURITY hive alone yields ciphertext — the exporting tool still has to perform the boot-key-derived decryption offline, which is exactly what Mimikatz's lsadump::secrets module (and equivalents in Impacket/gsecdump) automates.

concepts.term: Why this is often a lateral-movement multiplier
concepts.explanation: Because LSA Secrets frequently holds service-account passwords, and the same service account is commonly reused across many machines in an environment, one host's LSA Secrets dump can hand over credentials with reach far beyond that single box — unlike a local SAM dump, which is scoped to that machine's local accounts.

procedure_examples.activity: Used reg save for offline LSA secret extraction.

detection_queries.title: LSA Secrets Registry Access
detection_queries.description: Flags non-LSASS reads of the LSA Secrets key; LSASS itself reads this constantly and must be excluded to avoid flooding.
detection_queries.query:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)

subtechniques.name: Cached Domain Credentials
subtechniques.overview: Windows caches the last several domain logons (DCC2 / MSCache v2 hash format) at HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Cache, under subkeys NL$1 through NL$10, so users can still log on when a domain controller is unreachable. Mimikatz's lsadump::cache module or the cachedump tool extract these; unlike NTLM hashes, DCC2 cannot be pass-the-hash'd directly and requires offline cracking. On Linux, AD-integrated hosts running SSSD or Quest Authentication Services keep an equivalent cache at /var/lib/sss/db/cache.[domain].ldb or /var/opt/quest/vas/authcache/vas_auth.vdb.

concepts.term: Why the cache exists: offline logon
concepts.explanation: A laptop that's off the corporate network — no domain controller reachable — still has to let a user log in with their normal domain password. Windows solves this by caching a derived hash of each of the last several successful domain logons locally, and only consults it when no DC responds.

concepts.term: How DCC2 is actually derived
concepts.explanation: DCC2 isn't a simple hash of the password. Windows first computes the standard NT hash (MD4 of the UTF-16LE password) as an intermediate value (this intermediate is what's historically called DCC1), then runs that through PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA1, using the lowercased username as the salt and 10,240 iterations, keeping the first 128 bits of the result as DCC2. The username-as-salt means the identical password produces a different hash for every account, and the 10,240-round PBKDF2 makes each guess roughly two to three orders of magnitude slower to test than a raw NTLM hash.

concepts.term: Why it can't be pass-the-hash'd
concepts.explanation: Pass-the-hash works against NTLM because a domain controller can verify an NTLM hash directly during authentication — the hash itself is the credential the protocol checks. DCC2 was deliberately designed the opposite way: it's a hash of a hash, salted and iterated, that Windows compares only against another locally-recomputed hash during offline logon. A DC never validates a DCC2 value at all, so there's no protocol to replay it against — the only path forward for an attacker is cracking it back to the plaintext password.

subtechniques.name: DCSync
subtechniques.overview: DCSync abuses the Directory Replication Service (DRS) Remote Protocol to make a non-domain-controller host impersonate a domain controller and request password data via legitimate AD replication APIs — no code needs to run on a DC at all. Any account holding the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All extended rights (normally only Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and DC computer accounts) can pull current and historical password hashes for any account, including krbtgt, enabling Golden Ticket forgery. Mimikatz implements it in the lsadump::dcsync module.

concepts.term: No exploit, no malware on a DC — it's a legitimate protocol call
concepts.explanation: Domain controllers stay in sync with each other by calling IDL_DRSGetNCChanges over the MS-DRSR protocol, asking a peer DC to send whatever directory changes it's missing. DCSync is simply an attacker's machine issuing that exact same call to a real DC. There's no vulnerability being exploited — the DC is doing precisely what replication is supposed to do; it just has no way to verify the caller is actually another DC rather than an attacker who happens to hold the right permission.

concepts.term: Why the permission is the entire security boundary
concepts.explanation: Since the protocol itself can't distinguish a legitimate DC from an attacker, the only thing standing between DCSync and total domain compromise is Active Directory's own access control: who holds the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All extended rights on the domain object. In a healthy environment that's DCs, Enterprise/Domain Admins, and specific service accounts like Entra Connect — anyone else holding it (misconfiguration, over-delegation, or a compromised privileged account) can run DCSync at will.

concepts.term: Why krbtgt is the real prize
concepts.explanation: DCSync can request password data for any account by name, but the krbtgt account is what makes it catastrophic: krbtgt's hash is the key used to sign every Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket in the domain. Once an attacker has it, they can forge a TGT for any user with any group membership offline — a Golden Ticket — without ever touching a DC again, which is why a confirmed unauthorized DCSync means treating the entire domain as compromised, not just the accounts actually queried.

subtechniques.name: Proc Filesystem
subtechniques.overview: Linux's /proc pseudo-filesystem exposes kernel data structures per process, including /proc/<PID>/maps (memory region layout) and /proc/<PID>/mem (a direct window into that process's virtual address space). With root privileges an adversary can scan every running process's memory for credential-shaped strings; even an unprivileged user can inspect their own processes. Mimipenguin and LaZagne automate this against browsers, sshd, and other services that hold cleartext credentials in memory.

concepts.term: Why a filesystem path can read another process's RAM
concepts.explanation: /proc is a pseudo-filesystem — its files aren't on disk, the kernel generates their contents on demand from live process state. /proc/<pid>/mem is presented as a byte-addressable file whose offsets correspond directly to the target process's virtual address space; seeking to an address and reading is functionally identical to a ptrace(PTRACE_PEEKDATA) call, just exposed through ordinary file I/O (open/lseek/read) instead of a dedicated syscall. /proc/<pid>/maps is what tells a reader which address ranges are actually valid to read before attempting it.

concepts.term: Same permission model as ptrace, including Yama hardening
concepts.explanation: The kernel enforces the same access check for /proc/<pid>/mem that it would for ptrace: a process can only be read by its owner or by root. Hardened distributions add the Yama LSM's ptrace_scope sysctl, which by default further restricts even root/CAP_SYS_PTRACE-capable processes from attaching to processes that aren't their direct children — meaning the practical detection surface is less "was /proc/mem read" and more "did a process with root or CAP_SYS_PTRACE read the memory of an unrelated, sensitive process."

concepts.term: What the scraping tools are actually pattern-matching
concepts.explanation: Mimipenguin and LaZagne don't understand each target application's internal data structures the way Mimikatz understands LSASS's SSP layout — they take a cruder but effective approach: they know that certain processes (sshd, gnome-keyring-daemon, browsers, VNC servers) keep credential material near predictable markers in memory (a preceding "username=", a PAM authentication buffer, a known offset pattern for a specific browser version) and grep the dumped bytes for those markers, similar in spirit to how a Sigma rule matches a known-bad command line rather than truly understanding intent.

subtechniques.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
subtechniques.overview: /etc/passwd holds user account metadata (UID, GID, home directory, shell) and is world-readable by design. /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is root-only (mode 0600) by default. An adversary with root or sudo needs both files together — commonly combined with the unshadow utility — to feed offline crackers like John the Ripper or hashcat, since the two files are interdependent for that purpose.

concepts.term: Why the hashes were split out of /etc/passwd in the first place
concepts.explanation: Early Unix kept password hashes directly inline in /etc/passwd, which had to stay world-readable because ordinary tools (ls -l, id, getent passwd) need to resolve a UID to a username without root. The 1980s/90s "shadow password" scheme moved only the hash into a separate /etc/shadow file locked to root (mode 0600), specifically so any logged-in local user couldn't grab every hash on the box to crack offline — /etc/passwd was left world-readable by design because it no longer held anything secret.

concepts.term: The hash string tells you exactly what you're up against
concepts.explanation: The second field of each /etc/shadow line is formatted $id$salt$hash, where id names the algorithm — $6$ is SHA-512crypt, $y$ is yescrypt (the modern Linux default), $1$ is the long-deprecated MD5crypt. That prefix is what tells an offline cracker which algorithm and cost factor to target, and it's also why modern distros using yescrypt or SHA-512crypt with high cost factors are dramatically more cracking-resistant than older MD5crypt hashes — unlike Windows NTLM, these algorithms are deliberately slow by design.

concepts.term: Why unshadow is a required step, not optional
concepts.explanation: /etc/shadow's hash field has no use without the account context in /etc/passwd, and /etc/passwd carries no hash at all — cracking tools like John the Ripper want a single merged line per user (username:hash:uid:gid:...). The unshadow utility just joins the two files on username into that combined format; this is precisely why this sub-technique is scoped to both files together rather than either one alone.

Threat actors executed cat /etc/shadow to harvest password hashes from exposed Ray clusters.
